Neonates of the Tricarinate hill turtle emerge from parchment-shelled eggs after an incubation period that varies with local thermal conditions, and hatchlings typically possess a carapace length at birth of approximately 3.3 centimeters [Lb = approximately 3.3 centimeters]. These newly emerged individuals, still reliant on residual yolk reserves during their initial days, exhibit a corresponding wet weight at birth of about 8 grams [Wwb = about 8 grams], a modest mass that reflects the energetic constraints of the cleidoic egg environment. Field researchers have noted that these young reptiles, once they transition to exogenous feeding, embark on a prolonged period of somatic growth that will eventually lead to the attainment of adult dimensions. The ultimate carapace length for females reaches 15.1 centimeters [Li = 15.1 centimeters], corresponding to an ultimate wet weight of 511 grams [Wwi = 511 grams], whereas males achieve a slightly larger adult shell length of 17.5 centimeters [Li = 17.5 centimeters], corresponding to an ultimate wet weight of 621 grams [Wwi = 621 grams], a pattern of sexual size dimorphism that is reversed compared to many other geoemydid turtles. This divergence in asymptotic size between the sexes has been linked to differing reproductive roles and energetic investments over the course of their lifespans.

Data collected from captive-reared cohorts maintained under controlled thermal conditions provide a detailed portrait of the species' developmental schedule. Individuals attain a carapace length at puberty of 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters], a threshold that is consistent for both females and males (11 centimeters) [Lp = 11 centimeters] and marks the onset of gonadal activation. This size-based maturity cue suggests that body size, rather than chronological age alone, serves as the primary proximate trigger for reproductive readiness in this species. At a constant ambient temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the age at first reproduction for females has been recorded as approximately 2,373 days after hatching [tR = approximately 2,373 days after hatching], a relatively late onset of breeding activity that is characteristic of a slow-paced life history strategy. This delay permits the continued allocation of resources toward structural growth and the accumulation of sufficient lipid stores to support the energetic demands of egg production. Such a protracted juvenile phase is consistent with the broader life history syndrome observed among small-bodied, substrate-hiding chelonians occupying stable, seasonal environments in the Indian subcontinent.

The maximum reproductive rate of Melanochelys tricarinata, derived from comparative data on the congeneric species Mauremys reevesii and measured under equivalent thermal conditions, provides insight into the species' potential annual fecundity. At a stable temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], nesting females are capable of producing up to approximately 9 eggs per year [Ri = up to approximately 9 eggs per year] during the peak of the breeding season when conditions are most favorable. This figure, while modest on a daily basis, represents a considerable annual output given the species' extended reproductive lifespan. Gravid individuals typically construct shallow nests in loose soil or leaf litter, depositing a small clutch of 1 to 3 leathery-shelled eggs per nesting event [N_R_i = 1 to 3 leathery-shelled eggs per nesting event], and field observations suggest that females may complete up to 3 distinct nesting events each year [F_R_i = up to 3 distinct nesting events each year] when prey availability and ambient temperatures are conducive to repeated vitellogenesis. This annual rhythm is tightly coupled with the onset of the monsoon rains, which presumably aid in maintaining suitable nest humidity and reducing the risk of egg desiccation during incubation.

Long-term mark-recapture studies have yielded critical data on the species' maximum lifespan and overall survivorship patterns. When maintained under seminatural captive conditions at a constant temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for the Tricarinate hill turtle has been estimated at approximately 5,840 days [am = approximately 5,840 days], which corresponds to roughly 16 years of sustained physiological function. This impressive lifespan, characteristic of many long-lived freshwater and terrestrial chelonians, is supported by a slow metabolic rate and a robust capacity for tissue repair, as well as by behavioral strategies that minimize predation risk during the vulnerable juvenile stage. Older individuals often exhibit signs of reproductive senescence, including reduced clutch frequencies and lower hatching success rates, but the species' overall demographic structure suggests that iteroparous reproduction over many years provides a stable mechanism for population persistence despite variable annual recruitment. The extended post-reproductive period observed in some captive females further complicates the species' life history profile and warrants additional investigation into the physiological mechanisms underlying somatic maintenance.

Comparative analyses with related geoemydid species reveal that Melanochelys tricarinata occupies a distinctive position along the fast-slow continuum of life history variation. Its combination of a relatively small hatchling size, a moderate carapace length at birth of 3.3 centimeters [Lb = 3.3 centimeters], and a correspondingly low neonatal wet weight of 8 grams [Wwb = 8 grams] aligns it with taxa that exhibit a Type III survivorship curve characterized by high early mortality but extended adult longevity. The ultimate carapace length achieved by adult females, 15.1 centimeters [Li = 15.1 centimeters], and the slightly larger male asymptotic size of 17.5 centimeters [Li = 17.5 centimeters] fall within the expected range for a species of this body plan. At a stable temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum possible reproductive output, estimated at up to approximately 9 eggs per year [Ri = up to approximately 9 eggs per year], together with the approximate 2,373-day delay before first reproduction occurs after hatching (approximately 2,373 days after hatching) [tR = approximately 2,373 days after hatching], illustrates the trade-off between current reproductive investment and the maintenance of somatic integrity that underpins the species' remarkable longevity of approximately 5,840 days [am = approximately 5,840 days] under identical thermal conditions.
